Sergei Prokofiev. A Soviet and Russian composer, pianist and conductor who was one of the major creators of twentieth-century music.

After leaving Russia following the 1917 Revolution to live in the West, Prokofiev returned to the Soviet Union in 1936. There he produced some of his most famous works under the pressure of Soviet arts censorship. He's celebrated for his dramatic ballets, his early Classical Symphony, the film score Alexander Nevsky, and the beloved children's guide Peter and the Wolf.

Peter and the Wolf, Opus 67, is a symphonic tale with a narrator in which characters are represented by specific instruments. Peter is played by the strings, the bird by the flute, the duck by the oboe, the cat by the clarinet, the grandfather by the bassoon, the wolf by three French horns, and the hunters' shots by timpani and bass drum. This piece became beloved by children everywhere.

Romeo and Juliet, Opus 64, is his celebrated ballet score. It's famous for the heavy, menacing Dance of the Knights, also known as Montagues and Capulets, which features a driving bassline and soaring saxophone. His Classical Symphony, Symphony No. 1 in D major, Opus 25, was composed in 1917 as a deliberate imitation of the style of Joseph Haydn, becoming a pioneering work of Neoclassicism.

Alexander Nevsky, Opus 78, is his score for Sergei Eisenstein's landmark 1938 historical film, featuring the dramatic Battle on the Ice scene. Prokofiev later adapted this into a concert cantata. Lieutenant Kijé, Opus 60, is a suite adapted from his film score for a satirical Soviet movie about a fictional soldier created by a clerical error. It's famous for its Troika movement utilizing sleigh bells.

Prokofiev died on March 5, 1953. In an ironic twist of fate, he died on the exact same day as Joseph Stalin. Because Stalin died that same day, all flowers and hearses in Moscow were confiscated for the dictator's state funeral, leaving Prokofiev's small funeral with only a few attendees and paper flowers. Prokofiev shared the brunt of the 1948 Soviet anti-formalism purges led by Andrei Zhdanov with his younger contemporary Dmitri Shostakovich.
